title: Gandhi’s Satyāgraha — resisting injustice without reproducing violence
when: The campaign began at a Johannesburg mass meeting on 11 September 1906, opposing the Transvaal Asiatic Registration Ordinance. Gandhi coined the term in 1908, adapting Maganlal Gandhi’s proposed “sadagraha.” Its methods and principles continued to evolve through 1914.
people: Mohandas K. Gandhi; Maganlal Gandhi, who proposed “sadagraha”; and Transvaal Indian residents who pledged resistance. Abdul Gani chaired the 1906 meeting.
origin: It arose amid colonial racial restrictions in Johannesburg’s Indian community. Gandhi developed it through organizing and Indian ethical vocabularies of truth and non-harm, alongside transnational political thought; it was not his solitary invention or a synonym for every form of nonviolent protest.
idea: Satyāgraha—“holding fast to truth”—joins resistance to a discipline of nonviolence. Rather than injure an opponent, practitioners openly refuse an unjust law, accept its penalties, and use their willingness to suffer to expose injustice and invite change. Gandhi distinguished it from “passive resistance”: for him it was not merely a weaker substitute for force, but a commitment to truth, love, and refusing harm. It could include civil disobedience and noncooperation.
relevance: It offers movements a way to contest unjust rules without reproducing harm, while asking protesters to keep their truth-claims open to correction. But voluntary suffering does not guarantee authorities will listen, and its costs can fall unevenly.
